title: Bone.land Resonance
logline: In Bone.land's honest timber hall, Mx. BoneWAP audits the wish and publishes the finding that ends BaneWAP's patience: the smallest wishes have the longest arcs.
epigraph: Skeleton first. A wish, like a roof, is only as grand as the spine that must hold it.
description: Chapter 10 of Lore.Land: Bone.land Resonance. Bone.land is the small constitution — the spine that holds when the veil shakes. Mx. BoneWAP, a pie of clean-boiled honesty, audits the egg's karmic momentum against the ledger of every wish ever spent, and publishes: grand wishes cost a generation of coincidences. BaneWAP stops pretending to wait.

content.text: Bone.land did not pretend to be theater. Its square-hewn oak beams rose into the morning like the ribcage of a sleeping leviathan, every mortise and peg left exposed to the weather, because this hall was the small constitution — the spine the land trusted to hold when the veil shakes. Boof trotted across the sawdust floor, and the whole valley heard the frame answer her arrival with one deep

children.text: — not slapstick, but the sound of a structure declaring itself load-bearing. And on a scrubbed trestle table between the anchor stones sat something new: a pale, plain pie, steaming faintly, ringed by open ledgers. "Mx. BoneWAP," it said, by way of everything. "Research. I audit momentum. Set the wish on the scale, please."

content.text: Where BaneWAP was hoarded berries gone bitter in a banker's crust, and BoonWAP served himself and was never smaller, BoneWAP was clean-boiled honesty: no sugar it had not declared, no filling it could not show. In Bone.land, even a pie keeps its joints exposed.

content.text: The egg went onto the scale. A weight slid, a beam settled, and a low note ran through the frame into Boof's paws. The finding appeared in gold: the smallest wishes have the longest arcs. Given the current, a small turn could travel generations. Force the whole river round a throne and the corrections would come downstream, roof by roof. Boof shook the ringing from her ears. It stayed in the wood.

content.text: Plaster sneezes. Oak does not. Grand wishes are plaster; small ones are the spine.
He hung from the collar-beam like a bright bat and knocked. The oak answered as law, and the pie below him signed it.

sections.figcaption: Bone.land: the small constitution, load-bearing — and now, audited.

content.text: BoneWAP did not whisper its finding to a council or fold it into a drawer. It published — copies nailed to the anchor stones, carried to the tavern, read aloud at the Watering Eye. Item one: the egg's wish, spent small and true, would run to one lent coincidence and a spare Thursday, and its arc would outlast every roof in the valley. Item two: the grand wish a certain bitter pie intended would demand corrections costing a generation of coincidences — a whole town's worth of luck, drafted without consent. People stopped to read with baskets on their arms and tools still in their hands. Some followed each line with a finger; some asked a neighbor to say it again. The finding traveled out of the hall in voices that sounded nothing alike. Boof heard one person stumble over a sum and another get impatient, then go back and help. By afternoon the paper at the lowest stone had softened at its corners. A child held it flat while an older reader finished. There was no bell to mark the moment the news became theirs.

The ink was wet when word came up the pass: the bitter pie had read the finding. He had understood it. He had stopped waiting. Boof felt the tremor before she heard the messenger's feet. Above her, the pegs held; dust drifted from a beam. She checked the sling.

content.text: "Is this where the trail terminates?" Boof asked the king-post. The Fool answered with a soft knock on the honest oak — no. An audit does not end a story; it removes the story's excuses. Everyone in the valley now knew what the wish cost small and what it cost grand, and one bitter pie had decided the arithmetic applied to other people.

She settled the egg deeper against her chest and turned south. Behind her, the timber answered the shaking with small creaks, peg to socket, joint to joist. Ahead, the road looked much as it had that morning. She went carefully.
